newsitem.title: Bulgaria: Bulgarian Socialists rule out early polls.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists rule out early polls.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Saturday responded to President Zhelyu Zhelev's refusal to let them form a new government by ruling out elections demanded by protesters who have besieged parliament for two days.
The government said 196 people had been treated in hospital after clashes on Friday and Saturday, including 18 members of the security forces. One officer was in a critical condition.

"The government of Bulgaria clearly states that violations of law and social order as well as immediate parliamentary elections at this moment are destructive for the country," a government statement said.

Zhelev said on Friday that in view of the protests, he would not ask the Socialists, who are half way through their four-year parliamentary term, to form a new government. Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21.
Security forces attacked protesters with clubs early on Saturday ending a 10-hour siege of parliament with what the statement described as "minimal use of force".
"The opposition allowed the illegal mass rallies to mutate into crude violations of law and morality," the statement said.
"Order was restored in front of parliament and the deputies were led out of the building around 2 a.m. with minimal use of force."
Crisis talks between Zhelev and political and security chiefs, including opposition leaders, ended without agreement on Saturday.

Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the opoosition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), warned they might no longer be able to control the protesters, who have staged six consecutive days of antigovernment rallies.
Zhelev, whose functions are largely ceremonial but who frequently criticises the governing Socialists, said he backed the opposition call for early elections.

"Early elections will take place this year one way or another. It is best for politicians to organise them and hold them in a civilised way as it is done in a European country," Zhelev said in a speech broadcast on national television. He urged politicians to start consultations from Sunday.
The UDF appealed for calm. "Don't be drawn into a gigantic communist provocation," said a message broadcast every half hour by private Darik radio.
"Belgrade has withstood for 50 days without being drawn into provocation," it said, referring to protests against the Socialist government in neighbouring Yugoslavia.
The Promyana (Change) trade union said miners in the Rhodope mountains and port workers in Varna would go on strike from Monday, and Sofia taxi drivers planned a protest parade.
Sofia university students declared a strike and unlikely support came from Bulgaria's tiny rump Communist Party, which issued a declaration saying it supported the protests.
Most former Communist leaders hastily re-formed as the Bulgarian Socialist Party in 1990.
Russia voiced its concern over growing tensions in Bulgaria, which it described as a friendly state once seen as an "island of stability" in the troubled Balkans.
A statement issued by the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow hoped the crisis would be resolved "through dialogue within the constitution and democratic traditions".
Protests took place in half a dozen Bulgarian cities on Friday. BTA said local authorities in the Lovec region, which groups four large provincial towns, had banned mass gatherings.

The confrontation, spurred by acute economic crisis, came after the governing Socialist Party refused to vote on Friday on a motion calling for fresh elections. The UDF walked out and urged a nationwide strike and civil disobedience.

What began with a human chain around the parliament building on Friday turned into a siege, trapping Socialist deputies. The demonstrators broke windows in parliament and smashed and overturned deputies' cars parked outside.
In the early hours of Saturday police moved in, using clubs and firing blank cartridges to beat a path into parliament to allow the Socialist deputies out.
